Therefore the dominant strategy is to rank schools in my true preference order so that, once the obtainable set is realized, I receive the most-preferred school from that set.

reasoning.Student C:
The mechanism's key property states that the set of schools I could possibly be matched with (my Obtainable Schools) is fixed given others' rankings and school priorities, and my submitted ranking cannot change which schools are in that set. My ranking only determines which school I receive within that fixed set — I will get the highest-ranked school among the obtainable ones.

Therefore I should rank schools in my true preference order. Placing a less-preferred school above a more-preferred one cannot expand the set of obtainable schools and would only risk getting a less-preferred outcome if both are obtainable. Although many applicants prefer y > x > w > z (making y and x more competitive), that only affects which schools are in the obtainable set — not how my ranking selects among them. Given my stated preferences (y > w > x > z) and my priorities at each school, the optimal submission is my true ranking so I secure the most-preferred school available to me.
